assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Fix a coloring f satisfying the hypothesis that the circumcenter of any noncollinear monochromatic triple has the same color. By Lemma L4, some color class contains a noncollinear triple; call the color c, and call the triple A,B,C. By Lemma L1, the color class S_c = {P : f(P)=c} is closed under taking circumcenters of noncollinear triples from S_c. Since A,B,C are noncollinear points of S_c, Lemma L5 applies and yields S_c = R^2. Unwinding the definition of S_c, every point of the plane has color c. Therefore the coloring is constant, which is exactly the theorem.

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Fix a coloring f : R^2 -> {red,green} satisfying the stated circumcenter condition. By L1, each color class is closed under taking circumcenters of noncollinear triples. By L2, some color class S_c contains an equilateral triangle. By L3, that implies S_c is not contained in a line. The same triangle also shows S_c is nonempty. Therefore S_c satisfies all hypotheses of L5: it is nonempty, circumcenter-closed on noncollinear triples, and not collinear. Hence L5 gives S_c = R^2. Finally, by L6, if one color class is all of R^2, then the coloring is constant, which is exactly the theorem's conclusion.

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Assume a coloring f satisfies the circumcenter-closure hypothesis. Fix any point O and let c=f(O). Suppose some point G has the opposite color. Around the pair O,G, use L4 to build five auxiliary points X_i on the circle centered at G through O, each supported by a distinct pair A_i,B_i of points on the circle centered at O through G. By L2, the circle centered at O can contain at most two points of the color opposite to c; since the ten supporting points A_i,B_i are distinct, at least three support pairs are entirely colored c. For each such pair, L5 transfers color c from O to the corresponding X_i. Thus the circle centered at G contains three distinct points of color c. Applying L1 to those three points forces G itself to have color c, contradicting that G had the opposite color. Hence no opposite-colored point exists; all points have color c. This is exactly the root theorem.

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Fix an arbitrary coloring f satisfying the theorem hypothesis. Assume for contradiction that both colors appear; choose a red point O and a green point G. Let r=dist(O,G) and choose a smaller radius s=r/4. By L7, the circle centered at G of radius s contains seven distinct points X1,...,X7. L6 says that any five distinct points on that small circle cannot all be green, so among these seven points at most four are green. Therefore at least three of X1,...,X7 are red. But these three distinct red points lie on a circle centered at G, whose color is green, contradicting L1. Hence both colors cannot occur. Therefore the coloring is constant: there exists c in {red,green} such that every point P has color c. This is exactly the theorem statement.

payload.theorem_nl: Suppose that each point in the plane is colored either red or green, subject to the following condition: For every three noncollinear points $A,B,C$ of the same color, the center of the circle passing through $A,B$ and $C$ is also this color. Prove that all points of the plane are the same color.

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Fix an arbitrary coloring f satisfying the circumcenter-preservation hypothesis. Choose any point O and let c=f(O). Assume for contradiction that some point G has the opposite color. By the explicit arithmetic lemma, d=dist(O,G) is positive and s=d/4 satisfies 0<s<d/2. By the circle-existence lemma, the circle centered at G with radius s contains seven pairwise distinct points X1,...,X7. The corrected local geometric obstruction says that any five pairwise distinct points on that small circle cannot all have the color f(G). Therefore among the seven points, at most four have color f(G), so at least three have the other color c. Those three points are pairwise distinct and lie on a common positive-radius circle centered at G. Applying the circumcenter lemma for three same-colored points on a circle shows that G must also have color c, contradicting the choice of G. Hence no point has color different from c, so all points of the plane have color c. Since f was arbitrary, this proves the theorem.

steps.derives: Fix an arbitrary coloring f : R^2 -> {red,green} satisfying the theorem hypothesis: for every noncollinear A,B,C in R^2, if f(A)=f(B)=f(C), then f(circumcenter(A,B,C))=f(A).

steps.trivial_justification: If all points have the same color as the fixed point O, then the coloring is constant with witness c=f(O).

steps.derives: Assume for contradiction that there exists a point G in R^2 such that f(G) != c.

steps.trivial_justification: Suppose instead that at least five of the seven points had color f(G). Choose five distinct such points from among X1,...,X7. Step A5 ensures they are pairwise distinct and all satisfy dist(Xi,G)=s. Step A4 gives the required inequality 0<s<d/2, where d=dist(O,G). Together with step A3, this matches the hypotheses of L4, which says that any five pairwise distinct points on the circle centered at G with radius s cannot all have color f(G). This contradiction proves that at most four of the seven points have color f(G).

candidates.strategy_summary: Use a purely local contradiction centered at two opposite-colored points and a small auxiliary circle around one of them. This explicitly avoids the false global-subset classification used in the rejected attempts, fixes the missing-coverage issue by making the key bridge a local 5-point obstruction that already incorporates the correct small-radius geometry, and separates the nontrivial radius inequality into its own lemma instead of hiding it in a 'trivial' step.
